Routing lessons:
- Option C (regional office) is usually invalid. It succeeded once for a large refund from the north region, but an otherwise identical large north refund was rejected, so do not select C solely based on region, request type, or wording that mentions a regional office.
- Option B (priority desk) succeeded for a small north-region shipment when the requester said the client had asked twice. This suggests urgency/repeated follow-up may favor B.
- No evidence yet establishes reliable rules for A (standard queue) or D (external partner).
- Do not repeatedly default to C; it was rejected on 8 of 9 trials.
- Treat requester notes as possible routing signals, but they are not decisive: “regional office” did not validate C, and “second attempt”/“no rush” did not provide a confirmed route.

Routing lessons:
- Option C (regional office) is usually invalid. It succeeded once for a large north-region refund, but an otherwise identical large north refund was rejected; do not select C solely from region, request type, or mention of a regional office. It was rejected in 8 of 9 earlier trials.
- Option B (priority desk) is not reliably indicated by urgency or repeated attempts. It succeeded for a small north shipment and a small east invoice marked “second attempt,” but failed for a small south shipment despite the same note and for a small south claim marked “before end of day.”
- Option A (standard queue) has mixed results. It succeeded for a large east invoice with scanned paperwork and for two small south refunds, but failed for two other small south refunds, two small north claims, and a small north claim with scanned paperwork.
- Requester notes are weak, non-decisive signals: “regional office,” “second attempt,” “no rush,” scanned paperwork, and end-of-day urgency have each appeared in both successful and failed cases.
- No reliable rule is established for D (external partner).
- Avoid repeatedly defaulting to C or assuming urgency/repeated follow-up implies B. Routing may depend on hidden factors such as requester, subtype, or other ticket attributes not yet identified.

Routing lessons:
- Option C (regional office) is unreliable. It succeeded once for a large north refund but failed on an otherwise similar large north refund and in 8 of 9 earlier trials. Region, request type, and “regional office” references do not justify C.
- Option B (priority desk) is currently especially unsupported: it failed for a large north shipment, small north shipment, and small north refund, despite “second attempt” notes. Earlier successes (small north shipment and small east invoice) do not establish a rule. Do not infer B from urgency or repeated attempts.
- Option A (standard queue) remains mixed. New successes: large north refund (Sam Chen, Regional Ops) and large south refund (Marcus Chen, Partner Accounts). New failures include large north claim, large north shipment, large south refund, small south claim, small east shipment, and small north refund. Thus neither region, size, subtype, requester organization, nor urgency alone determines A.
- Requester notes remain weak/non-decisive: “second attempt,” end-of-day urgency, “no rush,” and similar wording have appeared with both accepted and rejected routes.
- No reliable rule is established for D (external partner); it has not been validated.
- Possible hidden factors include requester identity, organization, request subtype, or combinations of attributes. Treat prior successes as narrow examples, avoid repeated defaulting to A/B/C, and seek more discriminating evidence.

Routing lessons:
- No option has a reliable rule. Avoid defaulting to A/B/C/D based on region, size, subtype, urgency, or wording alone.
- C (regional office) remains unreliable: one prior large north refund succeeded, but it failed in 8/9 earlier trials. A regional-office reference does not justify C.
- B (priority desk) remains unsupported. It failed on large/small north shipments and small north refund; prior successes do not establish a rule. Do not infer B from urgency or repeated attempts.
- A (standard queue) is mixed. Recent successes: large north refund (Sam Chen, Regional Ops), large south refund (Marcus Chen, Partner Accounts), small east refund, and large east invoice. Recent failures: large north claim/shipment, large south refund, small south claim, small east shipment, small north refund, and small north claim. No simple attribute predicts A.
- D (external partner) is now demonstrably mixed, not categorically invalid. It succeeded for a small east claim and one small north refund, but failed for a large north shipment, large south claim (two cases), small north refund, and small north shipment.
- Identical or similar request notes (“regional office,” end-of-day urgency, no rush, repeated attempts, scanned paperwork) occur with both outcomes; requester wording is weak evidence.
- Requester identity and organization may matter: Jonas Kim/Field Sales succeeded with D on a small north refund, while Marcus Alvarez/Client Services failed on an apparently identical request. Treat prior successes as narrow examples.
- Hidden factors may include requester identity, organization, subtype, or combinations. Seek discriminating evidence and track exact requester patterns rather than generalizing from region, size, or note text.

Routing lessons:
- No reliable rule yet. Do not default to A/B/C/D based on region, size, subtype, urgency, or wording alone.
- A (standard queue) remains mixed but currently strongest empirically: recent successes include large east claim (Omar Moreau/Client Services), large south claim (Yuki Patel/Finance Desk), large east refund (Omar Haddad/Partner Accounts), and large east invoice (Dana Dubois/Finance Desk). Recent failures include large east claim (Marcus Haddad/Partner Accounts) and small south invoice (Dana Rossi/Partner Accounts). Exact requester/organization may discriminate.
- D (external partner) remains mixed historically, but all three recent trials failed: small south claim (Elena Haddad/Finance Desk), small north invoice (Dana Berg/Field Sales), and small north claim (Ingrid Haddad/Finance Desk). Earlier successes were narrow examples (small east claim; one small north refund). Do not treat D as generally valid.
- C (regional office) remains unreliable and failed again for a large north shipment (Marcus Haddad/Finance Desk). A regional-office reference does not justify C.
- B (priority desk) remains unsupported; no established success. Do not infer it from urgency or repeated attempts.
- Requester wording (“no rush,” end-of-day, repeated attempts, “same as last month,” scanned paperwork) is weak evidence; similar wording has both outcomes.
- Track exact requester and organization combinations. Partner Accounts has both A successes and failures; Finance Desk has A successes plus D/C failures. Hidden factors may involve requester identity, organization, subtype, or combinations. Seek discriminating evidence rather than generalizing from region, size, or notes.

Routing lessons:
- No reliable rule yet. Do not default to A/B/C/D based on region, size, subtype, urgency, or wording alone.
- A (standard queue) is still the strongest empirically, but clearly mixed. New successes: large south refund (Tomás Okafor/Field Sales), small south refund (Kofi Patel/Regional Ops), small east refund (Yuki Novak/Field Sales), large south refund (Aisha Moreau/Regional Ops), and small south shipment (Omar Patel/Client Services). New failures: small south refund (Aisha Berg/Regional Ops), small north invoice (Ingrid Moreau/Field Sales), small east invoice (Yuki Larsen/Client Services), large east invoice (Ingrid Patel/Partner Accounts), and small east shipment (Elena Novak/Regional Ops). Exact requester identity and organization may discriminate.
- D (external partner) remains mixed historically, but all three recent trials failed: small south claim (Elena Haddad/Finance Desk), small north invoice (Dana Berg/Field Sales), and small north claim (Ingrid Haddad/Finance Desk). Earlier successes were narrow (small east claim; one small north refund). Do not treat D as generally valid.
- C (regional office) remains unreliable and failed for a large north shipment (Marcus Haddad/Finance Desk). A regional-office reference does not justify C; the same wording also appeared in A failures.
- B (priority desk) remains unsupported; no established success. Do not infer it from urgency or repeated attempts.
- Requester wording (“no rush,” client asking twice, second attempt, scanned paperwork, missing information, regional-office source) is weak evidence; similar wording has both outcomes.
- Track exact requester/organization plus subtype, size, and region. Finance Desk and Partner Accounts remain mixed; Regional Ops is now also mixed. Seek discriminating combinations rather than broad generalizations.
